title: Projects and outcomes
principle: A project is temporary work intended to create a unique outcome. Operations sustain an ongoing service. Define the problem before proposing a solution.
scenario: A team receives requests for a new onboarding checklist. Is this a project or routine support?
exercise: Write a one-sentence problem statement, expected outcome, and observable success measure.
question: Which is a measurable project outcome?
choices: Reduce onboarding rework by 30% in 90 days

title: The sponsor and the charter
principle: A sponsor owns the business case and decisions. A charter makes purpose, scope, boundaries, roles, assumptions and authority visible.
scenario: A project launches with a project lead but nobody empowered to resolve competing priorities.
exercise: Draft a one-page charter stating sponsor, owner, scope, exclusions, deadline, and success criteria.
question: Who resolves a scope-versus-funding tradeoff?

title: Stakeholders and communication
principle: Identify people impacted by change. Map influence and impact. Agree when decisions, risks and changes must be communicated.
scenario: A support team learns about a new workflow only on launch day.
exercise: Create a stakeholder map and a communication plan with audience, purpose, channel, frequency and owner.
question: A good communication plan starts with:

title: Scope and deliverables
principle: Define what is included, excluded, and accepted. Break outcomes into verifiable deliverables. Prevent uncontrolled additions.
scenario: A small reporting project expands to include a new database and mobile application.
exercise: List five deliverables, three exclusions and one acceptance test per deliverable.
question: What prevents ambiguous completion?

title: Schedule and dependencies
principle: Plan milestones based on actual dependencies and capacity. Separate duration from effort; track the critical handoffs and assumptions.
scenario: A pilot needs security approval before production onboarding.
exercise: Create a milestone plan with dates, dependency, owner and evidence of completion.
question: Which step should happen first?

title: Capacity and resources
principle: People do not become available simply because a plan allocates them. Make demand, constraints and tradeoffs explicit.
scenario: One specialist is scheduled across three simultaneous projects.
exercise: Create a lightweight capacity table identifying bottleneck roles, availability and alternatives.
question: A resource-constrained plan should:

title: Risks, issues, assumptions, decisions
principle: A risk might occur; an issue is already happening. Assumptions need validation; decisions need accountable owners and dates. Maintain a useful RAID log.
scenario: A vendor might miss delivery, and an existing integration is already failing tests.
exercise: Record one risk, one issue, one assumption and one pending decision.
question: Which statement describes an issue?

title: Execution and transparent status
principle: Report progress against outcomes, next milestones, blockers and decisions. Separate facts from forecasts; escalate early.
scenario: A milestone slips, but the status stays green because the team worked hard.
exercise: Publish a one-page status report with evidence, forecast, risk, and decision needed.
question: A credible project status report should:

title: Change control and governance
principle: Governance should enable proportionate decisions. Evaluate changes to scope, schedule, budget, quality, benefits and risk before authorizing them.
scenario: A new requirement adds six weeks and changes the project budget.
exercise: Complete a change request showing reason, options, impact, owner and approval.
question: Before implementing a major scope change:
choices: Just add it to the backlog

title: Transition, closure and benefits
principle: Project completion is not just launch. Confirm operational ownership, support, documentation, acceptance and later benefits measurement.
scenario: The new workflow goes live but no service owner or monitoring is assigned.
exercise: Write an operational handoff checklist, lessons learned and 30/90-day benefits review.
question: What makes a sustainable handoff?
